# SK5001 — Request data is concatenated into SQL

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A value that arrived from the request is built into SQL text that a command executes.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Security |
| Default severity | error |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.1 |

## Why

The injected text is not data to the database, it is source code. A single quote in a value ends the literal the query put it in, and everything after it is parsed as more SQL running with the application's own credentials — which is how one search box becomes `DROP TABLE` or a dump of every row the connection can see. The fix is not to escape the quote; escaping is a blocklist and blocklists are wrong at the edges, on every dialect, forever. The fix is to stop concatenating: a parameter is transmitted beside the statement rather than inside it, so the database never parses it as SQL and there is no edge case left to get wrong. Every client has the shape — `command.Parameters.Add`, Dapper's anonymous `param` object, EF Core's `FromSql($"…")` interpolated overload — and all of them are shorter than the concatenation they replace. ⚠ There is no fix on the diagnostic because the edit is not local: introducing a parameter means changing the text, adding a binding, and choosing the parameter's type, which is three decisions rather than a substitution.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var id = context.Request.Query["id"];
command.CommandText = $"select * from orders where id = {id}";
```

Write:

```csharp
var id = context.Request.Query["id"];
command.CommandText = "select * from orders where id = @id";
command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@id", id);
```

## When it does not fire

The rule reports only a flow it can prove inside one method, from a source declared in `taint.json` to a sink declared there, with no sanitizer between them. Everything else is silence, and the exclusions are large on purpose — every one of them is a case where a report would be *wrong*, not merely unwelcome. ⚠ A method parameter is never a source. A parameter's incoming value is whatever the callers pass, which is by definition invisible from inside the method, so treating "unknown" as "suspicious" would assert a vulnerability in code that has none: a private helper ending in `command.CommandText = sql` whose callers all pass a constant with `@name` placeholders and bind properly is completely ordinary, and every report on it would be a false positive. Interpolating a *constant* is not a finding either, so `$"select … from {Schema.VersionTable}"` is silent. ⚠ `Main(string[] args)`, `Console.ReadLine`, `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable` and `File.ReadAllText` are deliberately not sources, because the principal supplying them is the principal the process runs as — there is no boundary being crossed, so there is nothing to inject. Passing a tainted value through `int.Parse` or `Guid.Parse` sanitises it, because the result is not a string. ⚠ Inter-procedural flow is out of scope (docs/plan/08), so a value that reaches the sink through a helper method is a miss rather than a report; so is a sink inside a lambda. Both are the safe direction for a rule that defaults to `error`.
